# Character.AI export viewer

Open your Character.AI data export and read your characters and chats — in your own browser. The file is read on your device; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Use it online, free and without an account: amavie.ai/character-ai-export . This repository is the same reader as open source, so you can check what it does with your file or run it yourself.

## What it opens

- Character.AI data export — the ZIP (or the JSON files inside it) from Character.AI's “Export data”: your characters and every chat, with dates and both sides of the conversation.

- Character cards — PNG cards with the card inside (SillyTavern, Chub, JanitorAI, RisuAI, Agnai, Backyard AI) and card JSON.

- Chat exports — SillyTavern .jsonl chats, WhatsApp and Telegram exports, plain text.

## Run it yourself

npm install npm run dev # opens the viewer at http://localhost:5173 npm test # format tests npm run build # static files in dist/ — host them anywhere

Requires Node.js 20 or newer. No server, no analytics, no network requests: the page reads the file with the File API and unzips it with fflate .

## Use the reader in your own code

import { readImportFile } from './src/lib/parse' ; const reading = await readImportFile ( file ) ; // a File from <input type="file"> if ( reading . kind === 'pick' ) { // Character.AI export: reading.pick.characters, reading.pick.chats (messages with role, name, text, time) } else if ( reading . kind === 'request' ) { // one card or one chat: reading.request.card_json, reading.request.chat }

## Where it comes from

The reader is the one Amavie uses to bring a character and a conversation over from another app; src/lib is mirrored from Amavie's codebase, so fixes land there first. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Amavie is a universe of AI characters who remember you and live their own lives — chat with them and play roleplay scenes on the web , iOS and Android.

Treat it as research code, not production-ready software. It may still contain bugs, and its coding style and engineering practices may be inconsistent. Some designs discussed in the article are directions for future development and are not implemented in this prototype.

dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person.

It is also a way of working with an agent: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use a result. docs/000-philosophy.md explains the principle and what it asks of the operator.

## Setup

Setup has many steps, so an agent does it with you. Ask your coding agent:

> Read SETUP.md in this repository and set up dsh-superagent with me.

It asks one short question at a time, shows the full plan once, and then installs and configures everything. SETUP.md is what it follows.

Read the numbered documents in order; each builds only on the ones before it.

- 006 Deployment : manual setup, configuration, upgrades and troubleshooting

# team-solve

A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a Memdoor workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of GVS5H (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of 9.8 of 10 over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone ( below , every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

## Five passes on the authors' ten (2026-10-31)

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files ( q38_multiagent_pN , fable5_single_pN ), the numbers in their paper. bench/results/parity-5pass/ holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read <scratch> and $HOME ; nothing else in the runs is edited.

Same as the authors'. Every message, byte for byte: lib/test_parity.py runs their multiagent_solve and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

Different. The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept ( log/host-switch.txt ).

What it took. The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, top_p / top_k on a model line, mark_cutoff for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

Where it lost. Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

- Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the case.

- Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8, arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most expensive runs.

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

## Run it

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/ # the library: any project sees it mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes

/workflow in memdoor tui draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out files beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin, compared to the samples with diff . It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's .memdoor/workflows/ . The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one included ( memdoor connect local for janis, Ollama or llama-server).

## How it works

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify └── ideate-b ──┘

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat". The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict:

type: command requires: - table_pattern: repair command: | check=.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh [ -f "$check" ] || check="$HOME/.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh" bash "$check" > final-test-output.log 2>&1 result=$? cat final-test-output.log exit "$result"

Each step is one YAML file in steps/ , the format of mario , the engine underneath. requires: is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt.

## What the first run found

The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder through OpenRouter:

- 8 of 8 steps, 5 of 5 samples. The solver took ideator A's prefix-state method, O(N) with a dictionary of (a−b, a−c) pairs. A brute force on 300 random strings found no mismatch afterwards, and it runs in 0.04 s at N = 200,000. The manager found nothing to repair.

- One ideator's provider dropped the stream mid-answer. The coder had written max_retries: 0 , so the run died there. The agent steps now carry max_retries: 1 , and the run was resumed with --partition , which kept the planner's and the other ideator's work.

- The ideator prompts the coder wrote named the sample's methods (A: a streaming prefix-state count, B: sorting prefix states), which would steer any other problem the wrong way. They now ask A for the most direct provable algorithm and B for one from a different family of technique (2026-10-28).

- The first attempts failed every step in 0 s with "no agent named coder": a run looked its agent up only in its own workspace. That was fixed in the gateway the same day (v1.692.0).

# bootgpt

A neural network that boots your PC.

The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS, no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log: timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.

Build thread: https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757

With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality you get:

[ 2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine [ 1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg [ 0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ... [ 1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212 [ 1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16

## Run it

brew install nasm qemu python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install numpy ./build.sh ./run.sh

disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.

## Pieces

corpus_gen.py makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.

train.py trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax) and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be diffed. They match char for char.

boot.asm is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.

record.py records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor socket. No window involved.

The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS plumbing into 510 bytes.

## Prior art

The boot sector genre is old and glorious. Oscar Toledo put chess , a whole OS and even a BASIC interpreter in there, other people did a C compiler , all inside 512 bytes. His book on boot sector games is a good read.

The closest neighbor is sectorllm , which boots a real llama2 transformer (5 layers, attention, the works) from about 1.2 KB of real mode asm, running Karpathy's stories260K model. sectorlisp-nn runs a TensorFlow-trained network during boot on a Lisp interpreter, and there are UEFI apps that boot straight into llama-class models on modern hardware.

bootgpt takes the other extreme: the whole engine fits in the 510-byte MBR itself, weights and strings live in the following sectors, and the model is not a general story teller but a tiny char-level net trained for exactly one thing, hallucinating the boot log of the machine it wakes up on.
